summary: The developer can start building the Python + LangChain multi-agent sample now: the machine has Python, pip, Node/npx, Docker, the documentdb MCP server, and the Microsoft Learn documentation MCP available, and many DocumentDB-specific agent skills are installed. Important facts the builder must not assume from memory were either outdated or incorrect (connection-string shape and ports, AAD data-plane support, vector and search index commands, billing model, local gateway image). None of those gaps block a sample that uses the live cluster and standard Mongo drivers, but the builder must follow the cited Learn pages and the installed DocumentDB skills. Add mongosh to the PATH if interactive verification is desired and ensure the LLM/embedding provider and embedding dimension are chosen and documented before creating vector indexes.
summary_points: Overall readiness: ready_with_gaps — all practical build tools for this sample are present and the DocumentDB data-plane MCP server + many DocumentDB skills are installed.

Critical factual corrections required before coding: use the documented DocumentDB connection string forms and ports (mongodb+srv to <cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com and non-SRV ports start at 10260), and use the cluster's supported auth modes (including Microsoft Entra ID / OIDC) — do not reuse Cosmos-account connection-string options such as replicaSet=globaldb or port 10255.
Bicep/Terraform/azd are not installed but are not required for this sample because provisioning is forbidden by policy; mongosh is not installed and would materially help interactive verification.

Vector indexes and full-text search are supported natively (IVF/HNSW/DiskANN and BM25 via createSearchIndexes/$search), but the builder must pick an embedding model and dimension to match the index parameters before creating vector indexes.

The installed DocumentDB skills (data-modeling, driver, vector-search, indexing, local-deployment, etc.) plus the documentdb MCP server and Microsoft Learn server provide authoritative guidance and verification tools for the build.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for a managed MongoDB-style cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (ARM type). Example ARM/Bicep reference: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters/<clusterName>. (If using the legacy Cosmos DB account surface the canonical resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the ARM/Bicep resource type for the managed MongoDB cluster surface is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters. (The older Cosmos DB account type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts remains for the Cosmos DB account surface.)

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2026-06-01 (deployment-language-bicep)

confusions.build_risk: None for this fact; using mongoClusters in ARM/Bicep is correct.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the az cosmosdb command group for the older CosmosDB account surface (core CLI). For the newer DocumentDB-managed MongoDB clusters the command group is az documentdb (or az cosmosdb mongo) which is provided by the Azure CLI extension named azure-documentdb or documentdb-preview in preview installs. Example: az documentdb mongo create --resource-group rg --name myCluster --location eastus --sku M30
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the az documentdb mongocluster command group (e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create / az documentdb mongocluster show). The az documentdb command group is the documented CLI surface for mongoClusters; historical surface names (az cosmosdb) are separate and may still have overlap but the current docs reference az documentdb mongocluster commands.

Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Multiple CLI command groups historically existed (az cosmosdb for Cosmos accounts, and extension-provided groups) and the product has evolved; older docs and extensions used 'cosmosdb' or extension names and some samples still reference them.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses an incorrect CLI group (or an extension that is not installed), automation scripts or verification commands may fail. e.g. running az cosmosdb mongocluster create when the environment expects az documentdb mongocluster could error or call a different resource surface.
improvements: Make the CLI quickstart page (Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI) say explicitly: "use az documentdb mongocluster ..." and note legacy az cosmosdb alias if present.
Add a short note in the documentdb MCP skill that the supported group is az documentdb mongocluster and that older 'az cosmosdb' references are legacy to avoid agent confusion.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (or, for the legacy Cosmos surface, Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts with kind: 'MongoDB'). Example Bicep snippet: resource cluster 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters@2024-01-01' = { name: 'myCluster' location: 'eastus' properties: { sku: { name: 'M30' } } }. Terraform: use azurerm_cosmosdb_account for Cosmos DB Mongo API (azurerm_cosmosdb_account with kind = 'MongoDB' and api_properties) or a preview provider resource named azurerm_documentdb_mongo_cluster / azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_cluster in newer provider versions. Example: resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "myaccount" location = "East US" offer_type = "Standard" kind = "MongoDB" ... }
confusions.grounded_answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters is the canonical resource to create a managed MongoDB cluster (the Learn templates and AVM modules document usage). Terraform: the recommended path uses Azure Verified Modules / AzAPI or Azurerm provider AVM modules (terraform-azurerm-avm-res-documentdb-mongocluster) that create Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters through AzAPI or AVM modules; using azurerm_cosmosdb_account (the legacy Cosmos account resource) is not the right choice for the managed mongoClusters surface.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-07-01 (deployment-language-bicep)
terraform-azurerm-avm-res-documentdb-mongocluster

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB 'account' resource historically deployed Mongo API accounts; newer dedicated mongoClusters were introduced as a separate ARM resource and Terraform AVMs evolved later. Some migration docs and tools still refer to azurerm_cosmosdb_account which confuses the two surfaces.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong Terraform resource (azurerm_cosmosdb_account) or old AVM pattern would produce a different resource type (Cosmos account) than the managed mongoClusters surface, causing mismatch with cluster features (vectors, cluster tiers) and possibly failures in verification scripts.
improvements: On the 'mongoClusters' ARM/Bicep docs add an explicit 'Terraform guidance' snippet: "Use the AVM terraform-azurerm-avm-res-documentdb-mongocluster module or AzAPI to create Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters" to prevent builders from defaulting to azurerm_cosmosdb_account.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Use a MongoDB-style connection string. Scheme: mongodb:// or mongodb+srv://. Host suffix for Azure-managed Mongo surface: <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com (or the cluster FQDN). Typical secure (TLS) port: 10255 for non-SRV endpoints. Required options: ssl=true (or tls=true), replicaSet=globaldb (on Cosmos surface), retryWrites=false (often required with Cosmos), maxIdleTimeMS=120000, appName=@<account>@. Example: mongodb://myUser:myPassword@mycluster.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000&appName=@mycluster@. For SRV: mongodb+srv://myUser:myPassword@mycluster.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/?ssl=true&retryWrites=false
confusions.grounded_answer: Wrong/mixture of surfaces. For the managed DocumentDB mongoClusters surface the canonical connection strings use mongodb+srv://<cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com for SRV and non-SRV endpoints start at port 10260 (then increment per node: 10260, 10261...). Required options include tls=true (or tls/ssl), authMechanism usually SCRAM-SHA-256 for native auth and MONGODB-OIDC for Microsoft Entra ID auth; retryWrites=false and maxIdleTimeMS are common options. The older Cosmos 'mongo.cosmos.azure.com' host + replicaSet=globaldb and port 10255 is the Cosmos-account Mongo API pattern and not the new mongoClusters surface.

Indexing, feature toggles and AAD auth options differ between surfaces so the app may not authenticate or reach the right endpoints.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary billing model is provisioned throughput in Request Units (RU/s) or serverless/autoscale RUs for the Cosmos DB-style surface. Some dedicated Mongo-style cluster SKUs expose vCore-based compute tiers (e.g. M-series or named SKUs such as M30) for dedicated instances; those are billed as compute tier reservations. In practice you will see RU-based billing for the Cosmos-style accounts and named SKUs/vCore for dedicated Mongo clusters (M30 etc.).
confusions.grounded_answer: The DocumentDB managed MongoDB cluster surface bills by compute tier (vCores/tier like M10/M30 etc.) plus provisioned storage per shard — it does not use RU/s. The RU/s model applies to Cosmos DB account (NoSQL) and the older Cosmos 'Mongo API' surface. Use compute-tier + storage calculations for DocumentDB clusters.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The two Azure product surfaces (DocumentDB managed mongoClusters and Cosmos DB RU-based accounts) are adjacent and share the DocumentDB/Cosmos DB naming history; the cold answer blended the two billing models.
confusions.build_risk: Choosing RU/s in automation or cost estimates for a DocumentDB mongoClusters cluster will produce incorrect cost computations and could lead to provisioning the wrong resource type or mis-sized resources.
improvements: On the pricing page for DocumentDB add a short line: "This is a compute-tier (vCore) + storage billed service; Cosmos DB Request Units (RU/s) do not apply to mongoClusters."

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Data-plane authentication for the MongoDB-compatible surface is primarily MongoDB authentication (SCRAM username/password or database users created in the cluster). Management-plane uses Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) via the Azure CLI / SDK. As of the current knowledge cutoff the MongoDB wire clients authenticate using SCRAM credentials in the connection string; full Microsoft Entra ID (AAD) data-plane token authentication is not generally supported for the MongoDB API. Use AAD only for management operations (az login, role assignments) and continue to pass MongoDB username/password to the driver for data access.
confusions.grounded_answer: Incorrect: the DocumentDB mongoClusters surface supports Microsoft Entra ID (AAD) for data-plane authentication via OIDC (MONGODB-OIDC auth mechanism). You can register a managed identity or AAD client and connect with a connection string that uses authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC (or MONGODB-OIDC/MONGODB-OIDC authMechanismProperties) as documented. Native SCRAM username/password is also supported. AAD is supported for data-plane access.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID (rest-api)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older guidance and some Mongo-compatible surfaces did not support AAD data-plane auth; the model defaulted to that historical pattern rather than the current DocumentDB capability (OIDC/MONGODB-OIDC).
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes AAD is not supported, they may embed credentials in connection strings unnecessarily or misconfigure authentication flows; conversely, attempting to use AAD without following the documented MONGODB-OIDC mechanism will fail.
improvements: Add a short example on the DocumentDB connection docs that shows both SCRAM and Microsoft Entra / OIDC connection-string examples and notes which driver options (authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC) to set.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: For application data access use the standard MongoDB drivers (for Python use pymongo, for Node use mongodb, for Java use the mongo-java-driver). There is no special DocumentDB-only data-plane SDK for Mongo operations; management/control-plane tasks can use the Azure SDKs (azure-mgmt-cosmosdb or azure-identity) but the app should use the official MongoDB client for reads/writes/vector queries.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use the standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo for Python) for data-plane access. For vector-search helper functions LangChain's azure adapter or the langchain-azure-ai vectorstore helpers are available, but the underlying transport uses the MongoDB driver.

confusions.build_risk: None if PyMongo is used; follow documentdb-driver skill for best practices (singleton client).

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: DocumentDB clusters support multiple ANN index types such as HNSW, IVF and DiskANN (example cluster SKUs advertise DiskANN + HNSW + IVF). The collection index is created with the MongoDB createIndex API using the knn/knnVector index specification. Example (PyMongo/mongo shell style): db.patients.createIndex( { embeddings: 'knnVector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', knnVector: { dimensions: 1536, method: 'hnsw', m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } } ). (Exact option names vary by server build; substitute engine:'diskann' or method:'ivf' and relevant params.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly wrong about the createIndex shape (it describes a community knnVector shape). Azure DocumentDB supports IVF, HNSW and DiskANN; the DocumentDB vector index API uses either the cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions style or the provider SDK create_index kind names (vector-ivf, vector-hnsw, vector-diskann) or the language bindings (langchain_azure_ai create_index). Example doc shows create_index via the SDK or a createIndexes-style JSON with "cosmosSearchOptions" (vector-ivf, dimensions, numLists) or the LangChain helper create_index(kind=CosmosDBVectorSearchType.VECTOR_HNSW...). Use the documented 'cosmosSearch' / cosmosSearchOptions JSON or the SDK wrappers — do not assume the community knnVector shape.

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used generic/other-Mongo-engine conventions (knnVector) rather than the DocumentDB-specific 'cosmosSearch' / createSearchIndexes / create_index patterns documented for Azure DocumentDB.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder attempts to create a vector index with the wrong command shape, index creation will fail. The builder must choose the index type and set the 'dimensions' to match the embedding model before creating the index.
improvements: Document the exact createIndexes JSON example for each vector kind (IVF/HNSW/DiskANN) on the quickstarts and make an explicit example for PyMongo + SDK and for the langchain_azure_ai create_index wrapper.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: You can use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({field: 'text'})) for built-in full-text search or push data to an external search service for richer features. On Azure, the recommended approach for advanced text/hybrid search is Azure Cognitive Search (index the documents or use a change feed) or a dedicated search service; hybrid search (vector + text) is implemented in the application by combining vector nearest-neighbour results with text-score filtering/boosting (or by using an external search engine that supports hybrid scoring).
confusions.grounded_answer: Wrong for DocumentDB: Azure DocumentDB provides native full-text (BM25) search via createSearchIndexes + $search (BM25-based engine) and supports server-side hybrid (BM25 + vector) retrieval patterns (Reciprocal Rank Fusion or server-side $unionWith) without needing an external search service. The builder should enable full-text search on the cluster and use createSearchIndexes/$search for keyword BM25 queries; combine with vector searches and fuse scores per the hybrid-search doc.

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB
Hybrid search

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer defaulted to the familiar pattern of using MongoDB text indexes or an external search engine (Azure Cognitive Search) which is common for many deployments, but DocumentDB provides built-in BM25 full-text indexes and server-side fusion primitives.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder sends text search to an external pipeline, they'll add unnecessary complexity and miss the native BM25 features and server-side fusion primitives; also they may misconfigure indexes.
improvements: Add a short 'Full-text vs text-index' note in the vector-search / full-text docs: "Prefer createSearchIndexes + $search for ranked BM25 queries; use $text only for legacy unranked searches."

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Clusters commonly support modern MongoDB wire protocol versions; an example supported server version is MongoDB 7.0 (MongoDB 7.x wire protocol). Common limitations vs upstream MongoDB: some server-side features and admin commands may be missing or behave differently (for example, certain server-side file system features, some aggregation stages with non-standard behaviour, or operator semantics). Transactions and change streams historically were limited on some Azure surfaces; check cluster documentation for exact supported features. Expect to use core CRUD, aggregation, and the new knn/vector features on supported builds.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly correct but under-specified. The service documents explicit MQL/operator compatibility tables and lists supported server versions including (example) 5.0, 6.0, 7.0, 8.0 wire versions depending on cluster configuration; DocumentDB supports most MongoDB operators but some administrative or server-only commands are not supported. Builders should consult the MQL compatibility page to confirm specific operators or aggregation stages required by their app.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer stated a single example (7.0) and hedged about missing features; the product actually documents the exact supported server-version compatibility matrix and operator-by-operator coverage which the builder should reference, so the cold answer was too vague.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes every MongoDB feature is present or assumes a different server version, an aggregation stage or administrative command may fail at runtime.
improvements: Link the MQL compatibility matrix more visibly on the quickstart page and in the documentdb-driver skill so agents consult it before generating advanced server-side queries.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no full local emulator for the MongoDB API equivalent to the Cosmos DB SQL emulator. For local development run the official MongoDB Docker image: docker run -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo -d mongo:7.0 (or mongo:6.0) and connect on port 27017 (mongodb://localhost:27017). If you need feature parity with the managed cluster (e.g. DiskANN vector indexes), test against the live cluster – those features are not available in the standard community image.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly wrong: while a plain MongoDB community image is an option for very basic CRUD testing, the DocumentDB project provides a Gateway Docker image and guidance for a local development gateway that emulates DocumentDB features more closely (gateway listens on port 10260 for Mongo endpoints). The documentdb-local-deployment skill and docs recommend a gateway Docker image and configuration (port 10260) for local parity; some advanced features (DiskANN) may still require the managed cluster, but there is a supported local gateway image for better parity than stock mongo.

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer defaulted to common practice (running an official MongoDB Docker image) but overlooked the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image and local-deployment guidance provided by the product for better dev parity.
confusions.build_risk: Using the community mongo image may hide incompatibilities in vector/search behaviors and port mapping differences; the builder should prefer the documented gateway image (or test on live cluster) for feature parity.
improvements: Add a one-line 'local dev' example to the main quickstart: if you need feature parity, run the DocumentDB gateway docker image (gateway port 10260) and link the local-deployment guide.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams are supported when the cluster exposes a replica-set-style topology and supports the required MongoDB server version. Use the driver watch() API (e.g., collection.watch() in PyMongo). On some managed surfaces change streams were not supported historically; if supported on your cluster no extra server-side toggle is required beyond having the right MongoDB version and proper user privileges. If change streams are not available on your cluster, you must use an alternative (polling, triggers, or platform-specific change feed).
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly correct but incomplete: DocumentDB supports change streams and provides additional features (resumability, historical replay) and a feature toggle for multi-shard change streams in the cluster 'Features' configuration (enable from the portal/CLI/Bicep). For single-shard setups change streams work using the driver watch() API. For multi-shard clusters, there is a documented enablement step and limitations.

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer reflected an older general rule for change streams and didn't mention the cluster 'Features' toggle required for multi-shard change streams in DocumentDB.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes change streams are enabled across the cluster by default, a multi-shard test may fail unexpectedly. The builder must check the cluster's 'Features' and enable the multi-shard change-stream preview when needed.
improvements: Add a short note to the change-stream docs: "For multi-shard clusters enable 'Change streams for multishard clusters' under Features; single-shard works without this step."

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: The dedicated 'documentdb' MCP server provides data-plane tools for inspecting collections, indexes and query plans for DocumentDB/Mongo clusters; it contains helpers that use the Mongo wire protocol plus provider-specific admin commands. The general Azure MCP server covers management-plane tasks (resource provisioning via ARM) but the documentdb MCP server is the right one for data-plane diagnostics and the mongo-specific utilities referenced by samples.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use the documentdb MCP server for data-plane operations. The azure MCP server remains available for control-plane tasks.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Microsoft used the name 'DocumentDB' for the original JSON document database service that later evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. Azure Cosmos DB is the multi-model, globally distributed database service that subsumed DocumentDB. The open-source DocumentDB project (a separate project) is unrelated. The modern 'DocumentDB' name in some docs can refer to either the historical DocumentDB engine (now Cosmos) or a newer managed MongoDB-compatible DocumentDB product – check context. In short: Azure DocumentDB/Cosmos DB are Microsoft services; open-source DocumentDB is different.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: there is naming overlap historically. Modern Azure DocumentDB (the managed MongoDB-compatible service) is a distinct managed service; Cosmos DB historically subsumed the original Microsoft DocumentDB; the open-source DocumentDB engine is a separate project. Builders must check context when older docs use 'DocumentDB' or 'Cosmos'.

grounding_links.title: Migrate from Amazon DocumentDB to Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Under the MongoDB-compatible surface there is a Microsoft-managed engine that implements the MongoDB wire protocol (on Azure this is the Cosmos DB compatibility layer or a dedicated DocumentDB managed engine for Mongo). From the application perspective you use standard MongoDB drivers and the Mongo protocol; differences come from server-version and feature mismatches (e.g., supported aggregation stages, transaction semantics, change-stream availability and performance characteristics). Expect to write MongoDB client code unchanged but validate any advanced server-side features against the target cluster.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the service implements the MongoDB wire protocol so standard MongoDB drivers work; application code usually needs little change but verify advanced features against the compatibility docs.

confusions.question: Which database name should the sample use?

confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the run-environment explicitly requires sample_healthcare_19.

confusions.question: What exact PyMongo connection syntax should the sample use to connect securely to the cluster from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI?
confusions.cold_answer: Read DOCUMENTDB_URI from the environment and pass it directly to pymongo.MongoClient. Example Python: import os; from pymongo import MongoClient; uri = os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']; client = MongoClient(uri, tls=True, tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=False). If the URI lacks options add ssl=true (or tls=true) and replicaSet=globaldb & retryWrites=false as required: MongoClient(uri + '?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false').
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly wrong: read DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it to MongoClient; include tls=true and auth mechanism options as required. Do NOT add replicaSet=globaldb — that's a Cosmos-account pattern. Use the documented options (tls=true, authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256 or MONGODB-OIDC for AAD, retryWrites=false and maxIdleTimeMS=120000 as appropriate). Use the DocumentDB quickstart's connection examples for exact options.

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed legacy Cosmos connection parameters (replicaSet=globaldb) with the DocumentDB surface. The general pattern of passing the URI to MongoClient is correct; the exact options must follow the documented examples.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder unconditionally appends replicaSet=globaldb or wrong port/options the client may fail to connect.
improvements: The documentdb-driver skill should include a single, copy-paste Python example showing: reading DOCUMENTDB_URI, passing it to MongoClient, and examples for SCRAM and for MONGODB-OIDC connection strings.

confusions.question: What vector index definition will the sample create for the patient record embedding field?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a knn/vector index on the embeddings field. Example mongo-shell command: db.records.createIndex( { embeddings: 'knnVector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', knnVector: { dimensions: 1536, method: 'hnsw', m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } } ). Adjust 'dimensions' to the model used and substitute method:'diskann' or 'ivf' if you prefer those engines.
confusions.grounded_answer: Wrong shape: DocumentDB uses the cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions pattern or the provider/SDK create_index with kind set to vector-ivf/vector-hnsw/vector-diskann and parameters like dimensions, numLists, m, efConstruction, etc. Use the documented 'cosmosSearchOptions' JSON or SDK examples and set 'dimensions' to match the chosen embedding model (for example 1536 for the OpenAI text-embedding-3-small model).

confusions.question: Which client library will the Python LangChain sample use for database access?

confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use pymongo for direct data-plane interactions; LangChain's Azure adapters (langchain_azure_ai or langchain's vectorstore) can wrap or assist vector/index operations, but pymongo stays as the transport for CRUD and queries.

confusions.question: How will the sample authenticate to the cluster when run in the developer environment?
confusions.cold_answer: The sample will use a MongoDB username/password-style connection encoded in DOCUMENTDB_URI (mongodb://user:password@host:10255/?ssl=true&... ). Store the connection string in the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI and never write it to disk. For management operations use az login and azure SDKs if required.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly wrong: the sample should read DOCUMENTDB_URI from the environment and may use SCRAM username/password in the URI, but the host/port and query-params should follow the mongoClusters patterns (SRV host or ports starting at 10260 and not the legacy 10255/replicaSet=globaldb options). The sample can also use Microsoft Entra ID/MONGODB-OIDC (managed identity) instead of embedding a password; choose and document the auth method in .env.example.

information_gaps.title: Pinned dependency versions for Python stack

information_gaps.title: Recommended index parameter defaults for small demos

The quickstarts give algorithm guidance but not exact 'safe defaults' the sample should use (e.g., numLists=1 for IVF or m=16/efConstruction=64 for HNSW).
